A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Distributed Speculative Inference and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D. The retained and revised material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original model-latency and acceptance-rate measurements, plus inference simulations reported in Table 1 and Figures 1 and 6.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D retain the original measurements and simulation results in Table 1 and Figures 1 and 6.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the rejection-sampling option, and the batching/lookahead procedure are unchanged. The added explanation about preserving the current verifier clarifies operation without establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate summarization on CNN-DM, instruction following on Alpaca, and code generation on HumanEval and MBPP. The simulated latency and acceptance-rate scenarios are also unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same SI comparator, and Figures 1 and 6 retain comparisons involving SI, non-SI, and their faster alternative. No evaluated comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: Section 4 retains the model pairs, 50-prompt latency sampling, generation lengths, A100 hardware, metrics, and lookahead/server grids. The revised theoretical processor bound does not change the reported experimental configurations.

E4.justification: The latency and acceptance-rate sweeps in Figure 1 and the fixed-lookahead analysis in Appendix D.2/Figure 6 are retained unchanged. No ablation, robustness test, or case study is added.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging five SI repeats per configuration in the simulation sweep. Seed information and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: All ten Table 1 rows retain identical latency, acceptance-rate, and speedup values, including the 1.29–1.92x DSI-over-SI range. Figures 1 and 6 retain the same heatmaps and findings.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces Theorem 2's proof sketch with a revised timing argument. Section 3.2 adds Proposition 2 on expected completion before SI with equal lookahead, supported by a new coupling and success-run argument. Section 3.1 also revises the processor bound. These substantially revise the theoretical support for the central speed guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and discussion retain the same claims about distribution preservation, avoiding training or architectural changes, and accelerating inference relative to SI and non-SI. Proposition 2 elaborates an already claimed advantage.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 newly explains that preemption preserves the guarantees by sparing the active verifier. Interpretations of the experimental results and the limitations concerning communication overhead, simulation-only validation, and resource consumption remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 revises processor-sizing guidance and adds the example that 5% drafter latency with lookahead 5 requires four processing units. It also explicitly identifies which threads may be preempted. Model links, prompts, hardware disclosure, SI code, and the code-release promise are unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography and research positioning are unchanged. Proposition 2 cites Leviathan et al. and Chen et al., both already discussed in v1.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the preemption explanation and theoretical exposition, with a small correspondence-footnote edit. The main narrative, section organization, experimental descriptions, and discussion are otherwise retained.

P2.justification: All six figures and Table 1 retain their content and design. Added theory causes localized reflow and relocation of appendix material; the SI listing is consolidated on page 20 instead of being split across pages 18–19.

improvement.justification: v2 provides clearer processor guidance and more explicit timing arguments, but the central theoretical revision does not clearly resolve v1's incomplete justification. The new coupling proof leaves the accepted-token count undefined when all sampled indicators succeed and ends with a particular success-run example rather than a complete general expected-runtime derivation. With empirical evidence unchanged, the net quality benefit of the theoretical expansion remains uncertain.
